answer:
Store it in the CRM. This is one of the few places where the model explicitly reaches out to GIS rather than deferring to it, and a surveyed polygon is exactly the payload it was built to take.

The class is E94 Space Primitive. Its scope note (as ratified under SIG Issue 390) says instances of it 'provide the ability to link CIDOC CRM encoded data to the kinds of geometries used in maps or Geoinformation systems', and the class's own examples in the v7.1.3 declaration include a GML <gml:Point> with an EPSG srsName and a Well-Known Text POLYGON ((30 10, 40 40, 20 40, 10 20, 30 10)). A closed total-station traverse serialised as WKT or GML, with its CRS named, is a well-formed instance. So the answer to 'was the model ever meant to hold this?' is yes, deliberately.

The structure to use, and the one trap to avoid:

1. The polygon string itself is an E94 Space Primitive. Carry the spatial reference system inside the serialisation (srsName / a CRS-qualified WKT literal) -- P168's scope note warns that definitions using different reference systems are always definitions of *different* places, so the CRS is part of the identity, not metadata.

2. That primitive defines a *declarative* E53 Place via P168 place is defined by -- a place whose identity is derived from its geometry. This is a new node, not your cut. The SIG is explicit on this: in Issue 391, 'If a place is defined by P168, it can only be declarative', and Martin's text behind Issue 390 says any geometric approximation of a phenomenally-defined place 'constitutes an instance of E53 Place in its own right, i.e., the approximating one.'

3. Tie that declarative place to the cut with P189 approximates (declarative place -> the cut's place). P189's scope note is written for precisely this documentation situation: coordinates taken from a survey or GPS 'do not state the actual place of the encounter spot but tries to approximate it with a "declarative" place', and the accuracy depends on the survey method.

4. What is at the other end of P189 depends on how the cut is already recorded. If your site database uses CRMarchaeo, an oval grave cut is an A3 Stratigraphic Interface -- the class covers interfaces 'formed by the removal or destruction of existing stratifications', which is what a cut is. A3 inherits from A8 Stratigraphic Unit and thence from CRMsci's S20 Rigid Physical Feature, which is declared a subclass of both E26 Physical Feature and E53 Place; S20's scope note says this multiple inheritance deliberately shortcuts the self-referential P156 occupies / P157 is at rest relative to loop. So the cut record *is already a place* and P189 can point straight at it -- no separate phenomenal-place node to invent. If the cut is only an E26 Physical Feature in your schema, insert P156 occupies to an E53 Place first and approximate that.

The trap: `connect A3 E94` will happily offer you P168 directly on the cut, because A3 inherits E53's properties. Do not take it. Putting P168 on the cut asserts that the cut's identity is derived from your polygon, which is false -- the cut is defined by its matter and its genesis, and next season's re-survey would produce a second, contradictory definition of the same thing rather than a second approximation. Keep the declarative place as its own node; you can then hang several of them (2019 total station, 2024 drone photogrammetry, a transformation into a different CRS) off the same cut, each with its own P2 has type and provenance, and none of them competing for the cut's identity.

Two honest limits, so nobody expects too much:

- The CRM stores the geometry; it does not understand it. The specification calls E94 'a primitive class for expressing values in data systems not further analysed in the CIDOC CRM' and adds that it 'is not further elaborated upon within this model. It is considered good practice to maintain compatibility with OGC standards.' There is no vertex, no ring, no coordinate class. Your area and orientation calculations stay in the GIS; what the CRM gains is that the authoritative outline travels with the record, is visualisable in context, and supports topological comparison between places computed from the geometries.
- Practically, E94 is normally implemented as a typed literal (geo:wktLiteral / ogc:gmlLiteral); Issue 391 closed on E94 being both E41 Appellation and E59 Primitive Value with RDF guidance to match. Robert Sanderson's objection when this was settled is worth knowing: 'Literals can only be embedded within the serialized graph, rather than referenced externally', his example being a 100+ MB coastline. A few dozen total-station vertices is nowhere near that scale, so the objection does not bite here -- but it is the reason a very large geometry might still sensibly live outside.

So: not a linked GIS layer, and not a compromise either. The outline goes in as an E94 Space Primitive defining a declarative E53 Place that approximates the A3 Stratigraphic Interface, and the GIS keeps doing the geometry.

rejected_alternatives.option: P168 place is defined by, attached directly to the record of the cut
rejected_alternatives.why_not: connect A3 E94 offers it, since A3 inherits E53's properties through A8 and S20, but Issue 391 states that a place defined by P168 can only be declarative, and Issue 390's background says a geometric approximation of a phenomenally-defined place constitutes a Place in its own right. Attaching it to the cut would make the cut's identity derive from one survey.

rejected_alternatives.option: P171 at some place within / P172 contains
rejected_alternatives.why_not: These are for places whose extent is not precisely known: a maximum extent the place falls within, or a minimum extent it contains. Both are declared shortcuts through an undocumented declarative place (search.py connect shows the full path via P89 and P168). The surveyor closed an exact polygon, so the direct definition plus P189 is the honest statement.

rejected_alternatives.option: E54 Dimension with P43 has dimension
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E54 holds quantifiable properties approximated by values with a unit - the area in square metres, or the orientation in degrees, would be legitimate instances. But a Dimension cannot hold the outline; it holds numbers derived from it. It complements the geometry rather than substituting for it, and storing only the area throws away exactly what the archivist wants kept.

rejected_alternatives.option: E31 Document / E36 Visual Item with P138 has representation, i.e. keep the plan as a linked drawing
rejected_alternatives.why_not: That models a depiction of the cut, not its extent. It is what the archivist is trying to get away from: the outline would remain an opaque attachment that no query over places could reason with, and P189/P89/P121 topology would be unavailable.
search.py concept E47 reports no definition in v7.1.3 - deprecated vocabulary. E94 Space Primitive is what replaced it; using it would be modelling against a withdrawn class.

rejected_alternatives.option: CRMgeo SP6 Declarative Place with Q10 place is defined by
rejected_alternatives.why_not: SP6 is a real and exactly-fitting class, and the pattern is identical. But E94 and P168 were pulled into CRMbase precisely to serve this need, and CRMbase's E53 plus P168 does the whole job without a second namespace. SP6 is worth adopting only if the site database already commits to CRMgeo's phenomenal/declarative class distinction.

siblings_considered.why_not: E95 Spacetime Primitive expresses geometries that are limited and varying over time, and it defines an E92 Spacetime Volume via P169. The total station recorded a static plan outline in a spatial CRS with no temporal bounding; the time-span of the cut is documented separately in the site database. A spacetime primitive would claim a 4D extent the survey never measured.

E92 Spacetime Volume is the cut's 4D extent, and P196 defines is quantified as necessary on it via E18, so the cut does have one. But E92 is not what a surveyed polygon defines: P168's range is reachable only from E53, and P168's own FOL excludes a place that is the spatial projection of a period. The polygon is a purely spatial extent, which is what E53 is - extents in space 'independent from temporal phenomena and matter'.

A2 Stratigraphic Volume Unit is the bounded body of matter - here it would be the grave fill, or the layer the grave was dug into. The surveyor traced the edge where the digging stopped, which is a boundary surface produced by removal of existing stratification: that is A3's definition, not A2's. If they also survey the top of the fill, that outline belongs to the A2 and is a different place.

notes: Two tool frictions. First, concept <id> prints a siblings block for CRMbase classes but not for CRMarchaeo/CRMsci ones - A3's siblings had to be recovered from the 'Superclass of: A7, A2, A3' line in concept A8. Second, quote accepts document chunk ids but the issue-page ids are not shown by the issues or issue commands; I only found the form issue391#current-s0006 by re-running docs with --kind issue --json. Three quote attempts failed on guessed id forms before that. The WKT POLYGON example I rely on comes from the v7.1.3 declaration printed by concept E94 and is not quote-verifiable, since E94 is not a document chunk, so I have not put it in quotation-marked citation form. On the substance: connect A3 E94 offers P168 directly on the cut, which is the opposite of what the Issue 390/391 record says should be done - the tool reports declared inheritance faithfully but the discrimination lives in the scope notes and the decision register, not in the connect output.
